title: Taizé chant
hook: a short line sung over and over until it sings you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the testimony service: people standing up to tell what God has done. Your line was God has been good. Who heard your good thing? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

How many times can a person sing the same line before it stops being words? In a small village in France there's a monastic community called Taizé, brothers from different churches living under one rule. Young people travel there to stay for a week, and in the evening they crowd into a long, low-lit church and sit on the floor. There's no sermon to speak of. A few voices start a line, short enough to learn in one hearing, and everyone joins. Then they sing it again. And again. Somewhere along the way, some who sing it say, you stop singing the line and it starts singing you. Today: Taizé chant.

A Taizé chant is built small on purpose. One line, from scripture or an old prayer, set to a simple tune. It's sung over and over, sometimes with harmony layered underneath and a single voice rising above. The words come in Latin, in English, in other languages, so that people who don't share a language can share a line. One of the chants sets the words of the thief crucified beside Jesus. In Luke's Gospel he says: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." That's the whole prayer. Sung slowly, many times, it has room to sink in. Now, an objection some raise. Didn't Jesus say, in the King James words, "use not vain repetitions"? He did. The same verse says what he's warning against: those who "think that they shall be heard for their much speaking." Many readers, including those who sing at Taizé, take the problem to be the vain, not the repeated, and point to Matthew's own Gospel. In Gethsemane, on his last night, Jesus prays to let the cup pass, comes back, prays again, and then, the text says, "prayed the third time, saying the same words." On his hardest night, he repeated himself. Here's why it can rest a person. When the line doesn't change, the mind can stop straining. It doesn't have to find the next word, or perform, or keep up. The line carries you, the way a boat carries someone who has finally stopped rowing. And a line sung that many times can stay with you. It may surface later, at a red light or over a sink full of dishes: a prayer that keeps going after the singing stops.

Here's the practice: sing one line ten times. Settle, and breathe. Choose a short line. If you pray, it could be the thief's: Lord, remember me. If not, any line that matters to you. Sing it quietly, on any simple tune, or just hum it. Then again. Don't count hard; let your fingers keep track. If your mind wanders, don't scold it. Just come back to the line. After the tenth time, stop, and let the quiet hold what's left. The bell holds the time.
Taizé chant. A short line of scripture or prayer, sung over and over, from a monastic community in France.

Your line: repetition is rest. Today, when your mind starts racing, at a red light or a sink full of dishes, come back to your one line and let it carry you a while. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: At Taizé, and in churches and student groups that borrow its style, prayer services center on short chants sung many times over, with scripture readings and a long silence, often by candlelight.

notes: No Taizé chant text is quoted (the chants are under copyright); the chant 'Jesus, remember me' is described only as setting the thief's words, with Luke 23:42 quoted from the KJV. Confirm the chant reference.

Description of Taizé (a monastic community in a village in France with brothers from different churches; young people staying a week; evening prayer seated on the floor; chants in Latin and other languages; harmony and a solo voice) is general and unsourced in the script; confirm.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): the narrator had settled the debate over Matthew 6:7 in its own voice ('The problem is the vain, not the repeated'); it now quotes the verse's own reason (KJV 'think that they shall be heard for their much speaking') and attributes the reading to readers who use repeated prayer. Some Christians still hear 6:7 as a caution against set, repeated prayers; a Keeper may want that view named too.
Original: βατταλογέω (Matthew 6:7, μὴ βατταλογήσητε); its exact sense is debated; confirm the gloss 'to babble, to heap up empty words'. The script avoids quoting 'as the heathen do'.
Gethsemane sequence (prays, finds them sleeping, prays again, prays a third time) from Matthew 26:39–44; confirm.

Editor pass: 'it starts singing you' framed as what some singers say rather than told to the listener; 'the objection someone always raises' softened; 'the mind can stop working' changed to 'stop straining'; 'and it will' cut from the practice.
